newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Army dissidence threatens Serbia's Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: Army dissidence threatens Serbia's Milosevic.

text.p: A threat of dissidence in the Yugoslav army emerged on Monday as a fresh obstacle to efforts by President Slobodan Milosevic to quell six weeks of street unrest against 50 years of unbroken socialist rule in Serbia.

A group of officers, including some from the elite 63rd Paratroop Brigade based in the southern city of Nis, warned Milosevic at the weekend that they would refuse to fire on demonstrators and could act against the government.

The officers' letter, read at an opposition demonstration in Belgrade and broadcast by a pirate radio in Nis, was unauthenticated and unsigned. There was no indication of the number of potentially rebellious officers involved.
It was addressed to Milosevic, Yugoslav Army commander General Momcilo Perisic and students at Nis University. Copies appeared to have been in circulation for several days before it became public.

The army planned to issue a statement later on Monday but the official Tanjug news agency said Perisic told Yugoslav President Zoran Lilic that it would continue to safeguard the stability of Federal Yugoslavia.
Whether genuine or not, the letter focused light on the disarray of the socialist government and Milosevic's difficulty in coping with the current crisis.
It indicated any attempt by him to declare a state of emergency would either fail or pit the army against Serbian police forces whose own loyalty is doubtful.

The army helped Milosevic put down demonstrations in 1991, but has remained neutral during his conflict with the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition which was cheated by the socialists of victory in local elections on November 17.
Political sources said a copy of the letter was handed to Perisic when he met senior paratroop officers in Nis during a tour of major garrisons to test the mood of officers and men.
According to newspaper reports, Perisic was told the army would disobey any order to open fire on civilians.
The letter urged him to "muster the courage, of which you once had plenty" and side with opposition attempts to win democratic reforms that would end one-party rule in Serbia.
Perisic was reported to have told Milosevic earlier in the crisis that the army would not help him but the officers' letter said part of the army was ready to go further.

"We will not allow Serbia to go under, we shall never act against our own people," the text said. "if necessary, we shall place ourselves at the head of the Serbian people in the final victory of truth."
The letter was not addressed to Zajedno and included a warning to the opposition that it would be toppled in its turn if it did not behave democratically in power.
The army has its own grievances against Milosevic who humiliated it at the expense of the police after the war against Croatian secession from former Yugoslavia in 1991-92.
Scores of generals were summarily purged and the army was run down while the police were reinforced with extra men and military fire power.

The letter was couched as a message to Milosevic "from the officers whom you denigrated so much and tried to turn into minor figures in this country, whom you denigrated in the 1991-92 war for which you bear part of the responsibility."

The ill-feeling against Milosevic did not prevent the army helping the Serb side in the Bosnian war when it provided the Bosnian Serb Army with a steady flow of arms, equipment and fuel to fight the former Yugoslav republic's Moslem and Croat-led independence.
It has remained strong enough to prevent Milosevic extraditing indicted Yugoslav and Bosnian Serb army officers for trial by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.
In former Yugoslavia, the army had quasi-independent status and was known as a "state within a state" which ran an exporting arms industry as well as acting as a guarantor of communist rule.
It was the world's fourth largest army -- in a country with a population of only 23 million -- and was second only to the former Soviet army in Europe.
